find: Python works with five primitive data types you must know, plus structured types for grouping data together.
replace: Python works with four primitive data types you must know, plus structured types such as string, array and record.
note: F1: the spec names four primitives; string is a structured type.

find: list all five primitive data types with one example Python value for each.
replace: list all four primitive data types with one example Python value for each.
note: F1: the revision tip must ask for four, not five.

find: The five primitive data types are: integer (whole number, e.g. 7 or -3), real (decimal number, e.g. 3.14 — Python calls this float), Boolean (True or False), char (a single character, e.g. 'A'), and string (a sequence of characters, e.g. "hello").
replace: The four primitive data types are: integer (whole number, e.g. 7 or -3), real (decimal number, e.g. 3.14 — Python calls this float), Boolean (True or False) and char (a single character, e.g. 'A'). A string (a sequence of characters, e.g. "hello") is a structured type, grouped with array and record.
note: F1: spec 6.3.1 lists string as a structured data type, not a primitive.

find: Beyond the five primitives, Python supports structured types that group multiple values together.
replace: Beyond the four primitives, Python supports structured types that group multiple values together.

find: Python has five primitive data types: integer, real (float), Boolean, char and string. Use the term real in written exam answers.
replace: Python has four primitive data types: integer, real (float), Boolean and char. A string is a structured type, like an array and a record. Use the term real in written exam answers.
note: F1: the takeaway must match spec 6.3.1.

find: Examiners award marks for meaningful identifiers when you write code — single-letter names (except conventional loop counters such as i) will cost marks.
replace: The specification lists meaningful identifiers as one of the techniques that make a program easy to read, so use them whenever you write code. Single-letter names, apart from a conventional loop counter such as i, make code harder to follow.
note: F2: replaces an invented examiner claim with the spec requirement.

find: Examiners penalise vague answers such as “it holds text.”
replace: A vague answer such as “it holds text” does not show the difference.
note: F3: removes a fabricated examiner claim.
F4: the sentence itself lists seven; spec 6.5.1 names seven.
F5: -1 is also a correct index of the last element, so it cannot be a distractor.

find: This is the fourth validation type and is unique to this specification — it goes beyond simply checking whether a value is present, the right length or in range.
replace: This is the fourth of the four validation types named in the specification — it goes beyond simply checking whether a value is present, the right length or in range.
note: F7: pattern checks are not unique to this board.

find: A simplified UK postcode check: the postcode must be between 6 and 8 characters, contain no spaces for simplicity, and start with letters before digits. A basic pattern check might verify: no spaces, at least 6 characters, and the first two characters are alphabetic:
replace: A simplified UK postcode check: with the space removed, a UK postcode is 5 to 7 characters long and starts with letters before digits. A basic pattern check might verify: no spaces, a length of 5 to 7 characters, and the first two characters are alphabetic:
note: F6: the prose said 6 to 8; the code below tests 5 to 7, which is the correct range.
F8: British English spells a computer program 'program'.

find: Always use the with keyword — it automatically closes the file and earns marks in “Write” questions.
replace: The with keyword is useful because it closes the file automatically at the end of the block. If you open a file without it, call close() yourself when you have finished.
note: F9: removes an invented mark claim and gives the close() alternative.

find: Edexcel is precise about the distinction — confusing them is one of the most penalised errors in exam answers.
replace: The specification is precise about the distinction, so keep the two terms apart in your answers.
note: F10: removes an invented examiner statistic.

find: Writing “a function performs a task” without mentioning the return value is an incomplete definition that loses marks.
replace: Writing “a function performs a task” without mentioning the return value is an incomplete definition.
note: F11: keeps the point, drops the invented mark consequence.

find: The most common mark loss in “Write a Subprogram” questions is a function that forgets to include return, or a procedure that accidentally returns a value.
replace: A common error in “Write a Subprogram” questions is a function that forgets to include return, or a procedure that accidentally returns a value.
note: F12: removes an invented mark-scheme statistic.

find: “A mistake in the code” is too vague for marks.
replace: “A mistake in the code” is too vague — it does not say which type of error you mean.
note: F12: removes an invented mark claim.
